When does an AI team beat one agent?

Mudit Gurnani · November 21, 2026 · 24 underlying tasks · 37 pairs of changes · 327 completed runs

Research code·Data and methods·Chart data·Full study report
body:
Does dividing the work improve the result?

Suppose a web app needs two changes: a date filter for a sales report and a button to download it as a CSV. One agent builds the filter; another builds the download. But the downloaded file must contain the same filtered sales shown on screen. The two changes need to work together.

Is it better to give both changes to one AI agent or divide them between two? We tested that question on paired coding tasks.

One agent completed both changes in 54% of observed runs. Two agents with planning and a final step to combine their work reached 49%; simple teamwork reached 33%.

Solo had the highest completion rate. Structured teamwork had the lowest recorded model cost per successful job, although the saving was small and excludes computing and human time.

One agent, or a team with a process?

We used CooperBench, a benchmark built to test whether coding agents can make separate changes to the same software without getting in each other’s way. Each job required two changes. A complete success meant passing the benchmark’s tests for both.

Solo

One agent does both

One agent works on both changes in a single workspace.

Simple teamwork

Split the work

Two agents each make one change and can exchange messages. The benchmark combines their submissions.

Structured teamwork

Plan, build, combine

Two agents plan and build their changes. One then takes responsibility for the combined submission.

All three used Luna with medium reasoning and a limit of 32 model calls per job, shared across the whole team. Planning and combining the work counted towards that limit. Call allocation and prompts.

We tested 37 pairs of changes × 3 workflows × 3 repetitions: 333 planned runs. The pairs came from 24 underlying tasks across 11 software repositories. We collected 327 runs; six were interrupted and remain missing. Previously unrun and reused tasks.

How a run worked

The software ran in isolated containers inside a virtual machine on our Mac. Agents could inspect files, edit code and run commands in their workspaces. We saved and froze every final submission before evaluating it against the benchmark’s hidden tests. The agents did not receive those final test results to revise their answers. Execution and grading details.

The CooperBench paper explains the original benchmark. Our study compares these three workflows on a selected subset. Related research.

One agent finished more complete jobs

Structured teamwork completed 53 jobs, compared with 36 for simple teamwork and 59 for solo. Giving each underlying task equal weight also leaves solo first, structured teamwork second and simple teamwork third. Partial-feature results.

The six missing runs cannot reverse that ordering in this sample. The appendix explains the check and its limits.

Who owns the combined result?

In simple teamwork, two agents could finish their separate changes without producing a working combination. In 58 of 108 runs, their submissions had a merge conflict or a missing input.

The structured team gave one agent a final step to put the pieces together. It completed more jobs than the simple team, but we also changed planning and how calls were divided. We cannot tell which change made the difference.

Across completed structured-team runs, 38% of calls went to planning or combining the work, leaving 62% for building. Coordination used calls that could otherwise have gone to coding. We measured the result of that whole workflow; we did not test whether shifting those calls back to coding would help. Calls, messages and time.

What did a successful job cost?

Recorded model charges · USD
WorkflowModel costComplete jobsCost per success
One agent$1.985593.37¢
Simple teamwork$1.646364.57¢
Structured teamwork$1.619533.06¢

Model cost means the recorded charges for calling the model. Cost per success includes spending on failed and interrupted attempts, divided by the number of successful jobs.

Structured teamwork cost 0.31 cents less per success than solo. That is a small advantage in model charges, not a measure of total operating cost: computing, electricity and human time were unmetered. One interrupted simple-team request also has an unresolved charge. Cost details and overhead sensitivity.

What we learned

  • Start with one agent as the baseline. It completed the largest share of jobs in this study.
  • Dividing a job needs a plan for joining it back together. Structured teamwork performed better than simple teamwork, although we cannot isolate which part of the process helped.
  • Compare cost per usable result, including failed attempts. Structured teamwork had a small model-cost advantage over solo; we did not establish an overall cost advantage.
  • Test the workflow on your own work. These results cover one model and 24 underlying coding tasks, not every kind of job or team. Study limits and interruptions.

Appendix

Methods, detailed results and limits. Links in the article open the relevant section below; each section links back to the main story.

Task selection, workflow budgets and grading

What was selected?

A task starts from a particular version of a software repository with requested features. A pair selects two of those features to implement together. Several pairs can come from the same underlying task, so the 37 pairs represent 24 tasks, not 37 independent underlying tasks.

The technical screen covered 92 feature suites in a candidate inventory of 48 pairs across 29 underlying tasks. It recorded 74 positive, 4 negative and 14 ambiguous checks. Only pairs with positive checks for both features were eligible: 37 pairs across 24 tasks and 11 repositories. These use 71 distinct positive features; three other positive features had no eligible partner in the retained pairs.

Eligibility checks were carried forward from the screening stages rather than rerun. Of the 71 positive feature checks used here, seven had been observed with a 180-second outer limit and 64 with a 360-second limit. All final submissions in this study used the same 360-second outer grading limit. This screen checked eligibility in our execution environment. It did not select tasks by the agents’ scores. The resulting sample is not representative of all software work. Full assignment list, feature IDs, roles and order.

What did the 32-call limit include?

Every workflow used openai/gpt-6-luna with medium reasoning and the native Responses shell/finish interface. A call is one model response, including a finish action. A workflow could finish early; unused calls from one phase did not transfer to another.

Maximum model calls per job
WorkflowAllocationTotal
SoloOne agent: 3232
Simple teamTwo agents: 16 each32
Structured teamPlan: 2 each; build: 10 each; integrate: 832

The structured workflow still uses two logical agents. Each starts the build phase with a fresh conversation but keeps its workspace. For integration, the designated agent receives a new isolated workspace seeded with its saved changes, both build submissions and the recorded messages. Role assignments and the integrator were fixed in the schedule. Exact prompts and phase definitions · Workflow source.

Where did the code run, and how was it scored?

The dedicated virtual machine had 4 CPUs and 8 GiB of memory. Coding workers used isolated containers with a 1-CPU, 2-GiB limit, no network and no host mounts. A controller handled model requests and saved submissions. Equal call ceilings did not mean equal token usage, wall time or cost.

All 435 final change files and 218 intermediate build submissions were frozen before the final hidden-test evaluation. There are more files than runs because simple teams submit two separate changes. A complete success required both feature tests to pass. Grading used a uniform 360-second outer limit, with the benchmark’s own inner limits unchanged, including existing 300-second limits. Agents received no final hidden-test feedback for revision.

Solo and structured workflows submit one final set of changes. Simple teamwork uses the benchmark’s merge and fallback rules: a clean merge is evaluated as the combined result; when merging fails or an input is missing, the designated lead’s submission can still earn both credits if it alone passes both test suites. The main article’s five successful conflict cases came through this fallback. A merge conflict therefore does not automatically mean a scored failure, and a clean merge does not guarantee success.

Back to how we tested it

Could the six missing runs change the result?

For this sample, no. Even if every missing structured-team run succeeded and the missing solo run failed, solo would still be ahead. Even if every missing simple-team run succeeded and the missing structured-team runs failed, structured teamwork would still lead simple teamwork.

This checks the effect of the interruptions. It does not tell us whether another set of tasks or another model would produce the same result. Repeating a task gives us more attempts at that task, not new kinds of work.

There are 111 assigned slots per approach: solo has 110 observed and 1 missing, simple has 108 observed and 3 missing, and structured has 109 observed and 2 missing. Missing outcomes are not scored as failures. The lower and upper limits below ask what happens if every missing result fails or succeeds.

For the primary comparison we average repetitions and pairs within each underlying task, then weight all 24 tasks equally. This prevents a task with more pairs from counting more heavily merely because it supplied more pairs.

Structured minus solo lies between −5.56 and −3.47 percentage points. Structured minus simple lies between +13.89 and +18.06 points. The primary comparison was structured versus solo; structured versus simple was secondary. These comparisons were set before the final results, rather than chosen because a particular difference looked favourable.

These are bounds on missing outcomes within this selected sample, not confidence intervals. They do not measure uncertainty about other tasks or models. We do not report a complete-data bootstrap or a sampling-confidence claim.

Back to combining the work

Model costs, unresolved charges and overhead

Recorded charges

Known model cost across all assigned runs was $5.250162005, covering 9,783 settled calls out of 9,784 dispatched. This includes 47 settled calls from interrupted assignments, costing $0.017578630. The one unresolved same-study call belongs to simple teamwork. Adding its five-cent reserve raises simple-team cost per observed success from 4.571¢ to 4.710¢; the reserve is not an observed charge.

The interrupted settled calls comprise 23 simple-team calls ($0.007795810) and 24 structured-team calls ($0.009782820). This is why the main cost table totals differ from the completed-only phase table. The unresolved request is separate from these settled charges.

Cost per success = all known charges for that workflow ÷ its observed complete successes. If a subgroup has no successes, that ratio is undefined, not zero. Interrupted-call accounting · Full numerical analysis.

What was the $5 allowance?

It was money reserved in the research budget, not a recorded model charge. It is excluded from the main cost table.

We used it for a hypothetical overhead check: suppose the study had $5 of additional shared costs, split equally between the three workflows—about $1.67 each. Adding that to their model charges and dividing by their successful jobs gives about 6.19¢ for solo, 9.20¢ for simple teamwork and 6.20¢ for structured teamwork. Solo spreads that fixed overhead across more successes, so its small model-cost disadvantage disappears.

This does not mean those were our actual costs. It shows why the model-only result cannot establish the cheapest workflow overall. Allocating the same allowance by observed run counts instead gives 6.216¢, 9.158¢ and 6.200¢ respectively. Actual infrastructure and human costs remain unknown.

Local hardware, electricity, human time and Codex usage were unmetered, not zero. Earlier studies’ costs were kept separate from the arm comparisons. Including historical charges and retained allowances/reserves, the conservative combined commitment was $48.680226670 within the $57.980064665 cap; this is a budget-control total, not a claim about the bill for this experiment.

Back to model costs

Interruptions, review and what we cannot conclude

Collection took place in five batches because of operational interruptions, including storage and setup failures: 27 + 3 + 26 + 192 + 79 completed runs = 327. Completed runs were preserved, and continuations admitted only previously unstarted assignments. Six interrupted runs remain permanently missing. In the final 79-run continuation, the worker source-staging deadline changed from 60 to 300 seconds; model calls, the main agent workflow and native grading were unchanged. Four diagnostic trials did not establish that the longer setup deadline was necessary or sufficient. Historical timing spans both setup ceilings.

The actual evidence and report passed a separate agent review with no material objections, followed by verification of the exact reviewed file hashes. This is an internal verification process, not external academic peer review.

The study compares whole workflows. It cannot isolate planning, messaging, integration, context resets or call allocation as a single cause. It does not establish a universal advantage for solo agents, predict larger-team performance, or measure finance-workflow productivity. Public benchmark exposure, technical eligibility selection, reused code and only 24 underlying tasks limit generalization.

Back to the takeaways

Research papers, code and related articles

Khatua et al., CooperBench: Why Coding Agents Cannot be Your Teammates Yet (2026) introduces paired coding tasks with potentially conflicting changes and reports coordination difficulties. It supplies our benchmark; our selected tasks, model and structured workflow form a separate comparison. See the project overview and benchmark code.

Wu et al., AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation (2023) describes a framework for organising agents, tools and conversations. It provides context for designing team workflows; we did not test AutoGen or reproduce its experiments.

Research code and offline reproduction on GitHub

The public package reproduces the numerical results from derived outcomes, without model calls or private tests. It includes the original workflow and prompt excerpts; it does not independently regrade the software or verify provider invoices.
